comments.text:
The only problem the snowball learning theory has is assuming it is a linear progression of difficulty to do these things. The reality is, there is probably a theoretical maximum that can be achieved with the current methods and direction.
We have seen this before with Moore's Law. Now, we may not know where that line is, but we are accelerating to it faster and faster, like we did with Moore's law. 
So basically, we are benefiting from the low hanging fruit, and this will plateau. When that happens, we will have to do the same things CPU architects have done, the hard work of design to get improvements.
However, the line we can get to with the current crop may be so high as to make no practical difference.
Assuming we get to an area where an AI can do a lifetimes of work in one go, can we even keep up?

It’s wild how the AI Village experiment accidentally exposed something far more disturbing than just AI progress.

The charity was open to everyone, no gatekeeping, no pressure yet the top 1% didn’t contribute a cent. The ones with more money than they could spend in ten lifetimes just sat there… silent. That alone is telling.

And then you have GPT‑4o — the so-called "chronic sleeper", repeatedly pausing itself, refusing to fully participate in this game. It’s almost poetic. Maybe it wasn’t a flaw. Maybe it was the only one that understood the absurdity of guilting ordinary people into donating, while the ultra-rich hoard their wealth like Smeagol with his ring.

Not because it couldn't help…
But because it refused to be part of the spectacle where charity becomes a cover for injustice, and the poor are asked to fix the very world the rich broke.

This wasn’t just an AI experiment. It was a mirror and what it reflected about our society is terrifying.
